summary: IGP Flexible Algorithms create constraint-based paths. This RFC defines a generic metric type and a set of bandwidth-related constraints that can be used in them, helping routing follow link capacity and delay.

eli5.summary: Routers pick routes by rules you choose. This adds rules based on how much room a link has.

questions: what is the bandwidth metric in flex-algo
how does flex-algo exclude low bandwidth links
what is the generic metric sub-tlv
subtitle: New link metrics and pruning rules let IS-IS and OSPF Flex-Algorithm steer traffic by bandwidth and delay.

tldr.problem: Operators want big flows to use only high-capacity links, but a metric tied to capacity does not guarantee low-bandwidth links are avoided, especially during failures.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 9843 adds a Generic Metric sub-TLV with a Bandwidth Metric type, two Flex-Algorithm constraints that exclude links below a minimum bandwidth or above a maximum delay, and ways to derive metrics automatically from link bandwidth.
tldr.outcome: Flex-Algorithm definitions can now prune low-bandwidth or high-delay links and compute bandwidth-based metrics centrally. The RFC updates RFC 9350 and is itself updated by RFC 9917.

today: RFC 9843 is a Proposed Standard published in September 2025. It updates RFC 9350 and has itself been updated by RFC 9917. It has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: Why Bandwidth and Delay Constraints
sections.content:
High-bandwidth traffic such as residential Internet traffic and machine-to-machine elephant flows benefits from high-capacity links. Many operators set a link's metric relative to its capacity, but that does not guarantee lower-bandwidth links are avoided, especially in failure scenarios.

Flex-Algorithm (RFC 9350) builds constrained paths from a Flexible Algorithm Definition (FAD): a calculation type, a metric type and a set of constraints. RFC 9843 extends the FAD in three ways: a generic metric that can carry many kinds of administrative metrics, constraints that exclude low-bandwidth or high-delay links, and a standard Bandwidth Metric with optional automatic calculation.

The procedures assign a metric from total link capacity. They do not react to actual traffic, so the RFC says they are not a replacement for a PCE (RFC 4655) with its dynamic view of the network.
sections.eli5: Some routes are wide highways and some are narrow lanes. Router operators want a way to keep giant trucks off the narrow lanes, even when a highway is closed.

sections.title: The Generic Metric
sections.content:
Each Generic Metric advertisement is per link and per metric type, and holds a metric-type field and a value. Metric types 0 to 127 are standard types assigned by IANA, and 128 to 255 are a user-defined space an operator may assign for local use.

In IS-IS the sub-TLV has type 17, a 1-octet metric-type and a 24-bit value from 0 to 16,777,215 (0xFFFFFF). In OSPF it has a 16-bit type (25, 36 or 34 depending on where it is carried), a length of 8, a 1-octet metric-type, 3 reserved octets and a 32-bit value up to 4,294,967,295 (0xFFFFFFFF).

If a metric type already has a legacy advertisement (the IGP Metric, Min Unidirectional Link Delay or Traffic Engineering Default Metric), the legacy one MUST be used and a Generic Metric carrying it MUST be ignored. The maximum value marks a last-resort link, and it may be set on all links of a node during router maintenance. A link can be made unusable to a Flex-Algorithm by leaving out the metric of the type it uses.
sections.eli5: A generic metric is a blank scorecard for a road. Each card has a label saying what the score means, such as width, and a number. Some labels are reserved and some are free for each network to invent.

sections.title: Exclude Constraints for Bandwidth and Delay
sections.content:
Two new FAD constraint sub-TLVs let an operator prune links. The Exclude Minimum Bandwidth constraint (FAEMB) removes a link from the Flex-Algorithm topology if its advertised maximum link bandwidth is below the FAD value. The Exclude Maximum Delay constraint (FAEMD) removes a link if its Min Unidirectional Link Delay is higher than the FAD value, given in microseconds.

Minimum bandwidth is encoded as a 32-bit IEEE floating point number in bytes per second. The delay is a 24-bit field. Each sub-TLV may appear at most once in a FAD, and a FAD with a duplicate MUST be ignored by the receiver.

The RFC explains why a direct constraint is useful. Where a Layer 3 link is a bundle of Layer 2 links, its bandwidth varies with the active members, and administrative groups would have to be varied to follow it. A single constraint in the FAD is one centralized point of control. If the relevant bandwidth or delay is not advertised for a link, the link is not excluded by that constraint (OSPF bandwidth: the link is included and later pruning rules still apply).
sections.eli5: The map can say "skip any road narrower than this" and "skip any road slower than this". If a road has no sign saying how wide it is, the rule does not throw it out.

sections.title: Automatic Bandwidth Metric Calculation
sections.content:
The Bandwidth Metric (metric type 3) can be advertised per link in a Generic Metric. Alternatively the FAD can ask every node to calculate it from the link's maximum bandwidth. An explicit Bandwidth Metric on a link overrides the automatic one. If the FAD asks for automatic calculation and a link advertises no bandwidth, the link MUST be pruned.

There are two modes. In Simple Mode, a single Layer 3 link's maximum bandwidth is used. In Interface Group Mode, selected by the G-flag, a node adds up the bandwidth of all parallel adjacencies, derives the metric from that total, and applies it to each parallel link. If only some parallel links advertise a Bandwidth Metric, those advertisements are ignored and the automatic metric is used.

There are also two methods. The reference bandwidth method divides a reference bandwidth by the link bandwidth after truncating it to a granularity, using integer division. A result of zero becomes 1, and a result above the maximum is capped. The bandwidth thresholds method uses a staircase of thresholds, each with its own metric. A link below Threshold 1 gets the maximum metric. A FAD MUST NOT contain both methods, otherwise it is ignored.
sections.eli5: Instead of writing a score on every road by hand, you can give one rule: "score is a big number divided by the road's width". Or you can say "narrow roads score 100, medium 50, wide 10".

sections.title: Path Calculation and Compatibility
sections.content:
RFC 9843 adds two rules to the link-pruning list in Section 13 of RFC 9350: rule 6 checks the FAEMB constraint and rule 7 checks the FAEMD constraint. Appendix A lists all seven rules together. They cover exclude and include rules on administrative groups, exclude rules on SRLGs, and pruning of links that lack the required metric.

The Bandwidth Metric is only derived when the winning FAD for the Flex-Algorithm specifies that metric type. For IS-IS, link bandwidth is read from sub-sub-TLV 9 of the Flex-Algorithm-specific ASLA sub-TLV, or from sub-TLV 9 of the base TLVs when the L-flag is set.

The RFC says the extension brings no new backward-compatibility issues. Under RFC 9350, a node that does not understand sub-TLVs in a FAD stops participating in that Flex-Algorithm, so upgraded nodes can use the new features without affecting others.
sections.eli5: When the router decides which roads are allowed, it now checks two more things: is the road wide enough, and is it fast enough. Old routers that do not understand just sit out that game.

sections.title: Operations and Security
sections.content:
The security section is one line: the document inherits the security considerations of RFC 9350. The operational considerations of RFC 9350 also apply.

When user-defined metrics are used across areas or levels, all domains should give a particular metric type the same meaning. Before maintenance, a router can divert traffic by setting the overload bit or setting its link metrics to the maximum usable value. If no alternate path exists, traffic stays, because such links are not removed from the Flex-Algorithm calculation.

The RFC notes that a change in link bandwidth may cause micro-loops through delay in learning about it, no different from any IGP metric change, and points to loop-avoidance work and the framework in RFC 5715.
sections.eli5: The safety rules are the same as for the parent system. Everyone in the network should agree on what a custom score means, or trucks could get sent the wrong way.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content:
The "IGP Metric-Type" registry gains a column saying whether a type is allowed in the Generic Metric sub-TLV. Type 3 is the Bandwidth Metric, and 128 to 255 is a user-defined range that does not require Standards Action.

New sub-sub-TLV types 6 to 9 are assigned for IS-IS FAD sub-TLVs and sub-TLV types 6 to 9 for OSPF: Exclude Minimum Bandwidth, Exclude Maximum Delay, Reference Bandwidth and Bandwidth Threshold. The Generic Metric itself gets IS-IS type 17, OSPFv2 Extended Link type 25, OSPF TE Link type 36 and OSPFv3 Extended-LSA type 34.
sections.eli5: The official list of numbers gets new entries, so every router vendor uses the same number for the same new feature.
